votes.plain_language: This vote confirms Keith Sonderling of Florida as Secretary of Labor. A Yea confirms him. A Nay rejects the nomination.

votes.question: Booker Amdt. No. 6835 — To establish certain standards with respect to coaches of varsity sports teams.
votes.plain_language: This amendment would have let coaches move between four-year colleges under transfer rules like those for athletes, and it would have voided a coach's endorsement deal unless the pay matched similar non-coaches and had a real business purpose. A Yea would have added those rules. A Nay rejected them.

votes.question: Booker Amdt. No. 6805 — To increase the limitation on funding for post-eligibility insurance and catastrophic injury for student athletes.
votes.plain_language: This amendment would have capped a student-athlete insurance and catastrophic-injury fund at $200 million and required major conferences and an athletic association to cover any amount above $100 million. A Yea would have set that cap. A Nay rejected it.

votes.question: Kennedy Amdt. No. 6760 — To limit price increases for college athletics tickets.
votes.plain_language: This amendment would have barred colleges, conferences, and athletic associations from raising ticket prices for a sport by more than 4 percent from the prior academic year. A Yea would have added that cap. A Nay rejected it.

votes.question: Paul Amdt. No. 6758 — To improve the bill.
votes.plain_language: This amendment would have replaced the college-sports bill with the Collegiate Sports Integrity Act, which centers on an antitrust exemption for athletic conferences and associations. A Yea would have made that swap. A Nay rejected it.

votes.question: Baldwin Amdt. No. 6828 — To modify the provision relating to the relationship of this Act to existing law.
votes.plain_language: This amendment rewrites the college-sports bill's preemption section so states generally cannot set conflicting rules on athlete publicity pay, transfers, or certain eligibility, while keeping state civil-rights, contract, privacy, and similar laws unless they conflict. A Yea adopts that text. A Nay rejects it.

votes.question: H. Con. Res. 89 — A concurrent resolution directing the President, pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution, to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran.
votes.plain_language: This House resolution tells the President to remove U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran unless Congress has declared war or authorized that force, while still allowing defense against an imminent attack. A Yea would agree to that direction. A Nay rejects the resolution.

donor_industry.caption: From itemized individual contributions over $200 reported to the FEC, grouped by the donor's self-reported employer and occupation. donor_industry.cycle_rule: The current term began 2023-01-03, so the most recent completed election for this seat was in 2022 (FEC two-year cycle 2022).

cycle_fields.calendar_period_note: This seat reports toward the 2028 election. Money dated 2025–2026 is filed under the 2026 FEC period and is not shown on this card yet.

stands_for.caption: Grouped by Congress.gov's official policy area. Shows how they voted, not why. Final-passage, amendment, and procedural votes can mean different things; read the note for each.

votes.question: S.Con.Res. 33, As Amended
votes.bill_title: A concurrent resolution setting forth the congressional budget for the United States Government for fiscal year 2026 and setting forth the appropriate budgetary levels for fiscal years 2027 through 2035.

votes.plain_language: This vote would end debate on H.R. 6938, which provides FY2026 appropriations to several federal departments and agencies for activities and programs related to commerce, law enforcement, science, energy and water development, public lands, and the environment. Cloture needs 60 votes (three-fifths of the Senate). A Yea limits debate so the Senate can move toward a final vote; a Nay keeps debate open.

roll_calls.question: Motion to Invoke Cloture: Motion to Proceed to S. 4668
roll_calls.result: Cloture on the Motion to Proceed Agreed to (74-24, 3/5 majority required)
roll_calls.plain_language: This was a vote to end debate on taking up a college-sports bill on athletes' name, image, and likeness rights, agents, transfers, and a limited antitrust exemption for selling some media rights. A Yea moves the Senate toward taking up the bill. A Nay would have blocked ending debate.

roll_calls.question: Motion to Proceed to S. 4668
roll_calls.plain_language: This vote starts formal consideration of the college-sports bill on athletes' name, image, and likeness rights, agents, and transfers. A Yea takes up the bill. A Nay refuses to take it up.

roll_calls.question: Motion to Invoke Cloture: Cruz Amdt. No. 6776
roll_calls.result: Cloture Motion Agreed to (70-21, 3/5 majority required)
roll_calls.plain_language: This vote would end debate on a substitute that rewrites the college-sports bill as the Protect College Sports Act, covering athlete publicity rights, agents, medical coverage, transfers, and college-sports broadcasts. A Yea limits debate on that rewrite. A Nay keeps debate open.

roll_calls.question: Amdt. No. 6776
roll_calls.plain_language: This substitute rewrites the college-sports bill as the Protect College Sports Act, covering athlete publicity rights, agents, medical coverage, transfers, and college-sports broadcasts. A Yea adopts that rewrite. A Nay would have left the earlier text.

roll_calls.question: Motion to Invoke Cloture: S. 4668, as Amended
roll_calls.result: Cloture Motion Agreed to (74-25, 3/5 majority required)
roll_calls.plain_language: This vote would end debate on the college-sports bill after it was rewritten as the Protect College Sports Act. A Yea limits debate so the Senate can move to a final passage vote. A Nay keeps debate open.

roll_calls.question: Baldwin Amdt. No. 6828
roll_calls.plain_language: This amendment rewrites the college-sports bill's preemption section so states generally cannot set conflicting rules on athlete publicity pay, transfers, or certain eligibility, while keeping state civil-rights, contract, privacy, and similar laws unless they conflict. A Yea adopts that text. A Nay rejects it.

roll_calls.question: Paul Amdt. No. 6758
roll_calls.plain_language: This amendment would have replaced the college-sports bill with the Collegiate Sports Integrity Act, which centers on an antitrust exemption for athletic conferences and associations. A Yea would have made that swap. A Nay rejected it.

roll_calls.question: Kennedy Amdt. No. 6760
roll_calls.plain_language: This amendment would have barred colleges, conferences, and athletic associations from raising ticket prices for a sport by more than 4 percent from the prior academic year. A Yea would have added that cap. A Nay rejected it.

roll_calls.question: Booker Amdt. No. 6805
roll_calls.plain_language: This amendment would have capped a student-athlete insurance and catastrophic-injury fund at $200 million and required major conferences and an athletic association to cover any amount above $100 million. A Yea would have set that cap. A Nay rejected it.

roll_calls.question: Booker Amdt. No. 6835
roll_calls.plain_language: This amendment would have let coaches move between four-year colleges under transfer rules like those for athletes, and it would have voided a coach's endorsement deal unless the pay matched similar non-coaches and had a real business purpose. A Yea would have added those rules. A Nay rejected them.

roll_calls.question: S. 4668, as amended
roll_calls.plain_language: The Senate passed the college-sports bill as rewritten into the Protect College Sports Act, covering athlete publicity rights, agents, medical coverage, transfers, and college-sports broadcasts. A Yea passes that bill. A Nay votes no.

financial_disclosures.caption: Official House financial disclosure filings from the Clerk of the House. A filing lists assets, income, liabilities, and trades the member reported; it is not proof of a conflict or of wrongdoing. Dollar ranges and asset names are in the PDF. This page links to the Clerk's copies and does not score anyone.
financial_disclosures.note: Senate financial disclosures are filed through efd.senate.gov, a different system from the House Clerk index used here. Senate filings are not listed yet.

funding.heading: Disclosed campaign receipts
funding.detail: Federal cards show the principal campaign committee and OpenFEC totals for one two-year cycle, plus itemized Schedule A contributors. House uses 2026. Senate uses the cycle of the next election (2026, 2028, or 2030). This is not career fundraising and does not include Schedule E outside spending. Governors do not get a federal contribution list.

town_halls.note: There is no national town-hall dataset. Dates are not estimated.

disclosure_note: Disclosed contributions only; donors behind groups that do not report their own donors are not in this feed.
vote_scope: This is not a full career record. The cache is the latest 40 House rolls (2026, rolls 275-314) and 40 Senate votes (119th Congress, session 2, votes 217-256).
